turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you to the clinic?
turns.patient_response: Well, I came in because... I just can't stop focusing on my jaw and neck. There's this sagging, uneven spot right around there, and it's all I can see. People tell me it looks normal, but I just know it's not. When I'm at work doing hair, or talking to the nurses, or even just at church... I feel like it's the very first thing anyone notices when they look at me. It's really starting to bother me.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent preoccupation with a perceived flaw in their jaw and neck that others state looks normal, believing it is immediately noticeable to others.

turns.doctor_question: How certain are you that the sagging and unevenness are truly noticeable to other people?
turns.patient_response: I'm very certain. I know people say it looks fine, but... I just can't stop seeing it. It's this sagging, uneven spot right around my jaw and neck. It's just so obvious to me. Even when folks try to reassure me, I still feel like it's the very first thing the families at the salon, the nurses, or the people at church notice when they look at me. I just can't get it out of my head.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent preoccupation with a perceived sagging and uneven spot around their jaw and neck that they cannot stop focusing on, despite reassurance from others that it looks fine.

turns.doctor_question: Do you repeatedly check your jaw or neck in mirrors, photos, or other reflective surfaces?
turns.patient_response:
Yes, I do. Um, before I leave for work or a meeting, I just keep going back to the bathroom mirror. I'll stand there fixing my collar, or moving my hair around my neck to see if I can hide it. Then I usually end up taking another look using my phone camera. 

Sometimes I'll even ask my daughter if it looks strange to her. Honestly, doing all that... it's made me late more than once.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient confirms engaging in repetitive appearance-related behaviors, including repeatedly checking the mirror and phone camera, camouflaging with hair and collar, and seeking reassurance from their daughter.

turns.doctor_question: Is there any part of you that can consider the possibility that the flaw may not be as noticeable as you believe, or are you completely certain it is obvious to others?
turns.patient_response:
I... I don't really know. I mean, since my daughter and other people keep telling me they don't really see it, I guess a small part of me wonders if maybe it's not quite as bad as I think it is. 

But... then I look in the mirror, and it just looks so clear to me. It's hard to believe them when I can see it right there. So, I'm just not really sure.

turns.doctor_question: If a trusted clinician examined your jaw and neck and told you there was no noticeable abnormality, would you be able to accept that conclusion?
turns.patient_response: I... I honestly don't know. I mean, if a doctor told me that, I'd want to believe them. I really would. But... I just see it so clearly every time I look in the mirror. I think it would be really hard for me to just accept it and stop worrying, even if a professional said it was fine. It's just so obvious to me.

turns.doctor_question: When other people or a clinician say they do not see a problem, can you consider that your belief might be mistaken, or are you convinced they are wrong?
turns.patient_response: I guess it's a mix of both. When people tell me they don't see it, I do try to consider that maybe I'm mistaken. I mean, they have no reason to lie to me. But... it's just really hard to fully believe them when I can see it so clearly myself. So I wouldn't say I'm completely convinced they're wrong, but I also can't just let go of what I see.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe there is any possibility, even a very small one, that your jaw and neck look normal to other people?
turns.patient_response: I mean... yes, I suppose there's a small possibility. If everyone keeps telling me it's fine, then maybe to them, it really does look normal. I try to tell myself that. It's just... even if I admit there's a chance they're right, it doesn't really change what I see in the mirror.

turns.doctor_question: How much does worrying about your jaw and neck interfere with your work, relationships, or daily activities?
turns.patient_response:
It interferes a good amount, honestly. Like at work, I’ve... well, I've passed up chances to help lead meetings or take on the supervisory pieces. I just worry too much that people will be staring right at my face and neck if I'm up front. And I’ve actually fallen behind on my paperwork lately, mostly because I get stuck in the mirror trying to make myself look presentable before I can even leave the house. 

As for my personal life... it affects that, too. I’ve stopped going to some of my book club and walking club activities. The whole process of getting ready and trying to look okay just feels like too much to deal with.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes excessive preoccupation with their face and neck, avoiding work tasks out of worry that others will stare at these features.
symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient engages in repetitive mirror-checking and prolonged grooming rituals ('get stuck in the mirror trying to make myself look presentable') to the extent of causing significant daily delay.
